entries.title: Reindeer butchery and early activity at Slotseng
entries.dateMeaning: Calibrated radiocarbon interval for the reindeer deposit
entries.summary: Worked flint and a concentrated reindeer-bone deposit survive near a Late Ice Age locality.
entries.detail: The deposit records hunting and processing near a seasonal reindeer route. Excavators identified flint scatters and evidence for several distinct activity phases in the area.
entries.uncertainty: The calibrated interval is the museum’s 95-percent dating range for the deposit. It gives no exact arrival year for people in Denmark.

entries.title: A submerged settlement and canoes at Tybrind Vig
entries.place: Tybrind Vig, western Funen, coastal anchor
entries.summary: Underwater excavations exposed a coastal habitation site with fishing equipment, wooden paddles and dugout canoe remains.
entries.detail: Submergence and waterlogged deposits preserve evidence of how people fished, traveled and made everyday equipment. The present shore is different from the shore they used.
entries.uncertainty: The dates describe the broad Ertebølle phase. Individual finds and layers have separate dates, and the marker is a bay anchor.

entries.title: Communities build enclosures at Sarup
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded dates of two distinct enclosure phases
entries.summary: Two large sets of ditches and timber barriers belong to separate Neolithic construction phases.
entries.detail: The scale implies coordinated work. Finds from the enclosures inform interpretations about periodic gathering, exchange and ceremony among dispersed communities.
entries.uncertainty: The dates belong to two separate layouts, with no claim of occupation in every year between them.

entries.title: Oak-coffin burial at Egtved
entries.summary: An oak coffin and a young woman’s grave preserve evidence of Bronze Age clothing, craft and burial choices.
entries.detail: Dendrochronology dates the coffin wood. Textiles, personal equipment and plant remains reveal materials that commonly disappear in other archaeological deposits.
entries.uncertainty: The precise date applies to the coffin’s tree-ring evidence and burial context. It cannot resolve where the person grew up.

entries.title: Tollund Man placed in a peat bog
entries.place: Bjældskovdal, west of Silkeborg, bog-area anchor
entries.summary: Peat preserved a person deposited in the Early Iron Age and provides evidence for clothing, diet and treatment of the body.
entries.detail: New radiocarbon analyses narrowed the estimated age. The stable date permits comparison with other Iron Age deposits without assuming an identical explanation.
entries.uncertainty: The range is statistical. The motives and entire sequence of events remain uncertain.

entries.title: Small metal-foil figures at Sorte Muld
entries.dateLabel: About 550–700 CE for the foil figures
entries.dateMeaning: Broad comparative dating of the excavated foil figures
entries.place: Sorte Muld vicinity, near Ibsker, Bornholm
entries.summary: Excavations and surveys around Sorte Muld have recovered thousands of tiny stamped metal-foil figures.
entries.detail: Gold and silver foils provide evidence of skilled metalworking and patterns of deposition. The settlement and other excavated objects have broader chronologies.
entries.uncertainty: The range is an archaeological estimate for the foils. The interpretation of individual deposits and images remains open.

entries.title: A marketplace at Ribe
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded start of archaeologically visible market activity
entries.summary: Archaeology documents an early eighth-century market with distinct plots and workshop activity.
entries.detail: People produced and exchanged objects around a river crossing and coastal access point. More permanent buildings followed the early trading activity.
entries.uncertainty: The date marks a broad archaeological threshold for the marketplace. Earlier visits and the length of seasonal activity are difficult to establish.

entries.title: Royal monuments and conversion claims at Jelling
entries.summary: Mounds, rune stones and a church mark a royal commemorative landscape.
entries.detail: The larger stone credits Harald with political achievements and Christianization. Its wording is evidence of what a ruler publicly claimed, while archaeology records building and burial practices.
entries.uncertainty: The interval summarizes the royal monument phase. Religious practice varied across communities and changed over a much longer time.

entries.title: Aggersborg overlooks the Limfjord
entries.summary: The largest ring fortress stands near a narrow Limfjord crossing.
entries.detail: Its presence beside an important transport landscape shows the geographic reach and variation of the shared fortress design. Earlier settlement remains are also known at the site.
entries.uncertainty: The mapped interval refers to the ring fortress project, separate from other archaeological phases there.

entries.title: Ring fortress building at Trelleborg
entries.summary: A precise circular layout with intersecting roads marks one of five recognized Danish Viking Age ring fortresses.
entries.detail: The building program concentrated timber and labor. Trelleborg’s location and design can be compared with sites in Funen and Jutland.
entries.uncertainty: The date is the archaeological construction cluster for the fortress series. Their functions and duration of individual use differ.

entries.title: Brick-building at Roskilde Cathedral
entries.summary: A cathedral was built in brick in successive stages on the site of earlier religious buildings.
entries.detail: The work required skilled building labor and procurement. Later royal burials, chapels and repairs changed the complex further.
entries.uncertainty: The interval refers to the medieval rebuilding phase, and surviving fabric has several dates.

entries.title: University of Copenhagen opens
entries.summary: Teaching began at a university established with ecclesiastical and royal authorization.
entries.detail: The institution gathered students and teachers into the late medieval city. Religious and political change later reshaped both its organization and its curriculum.
entries.uncertainty: The pin locates the university precinct. The opening date does not date the buildings seen there today.

entries.title: Ships entered in the Sound Toll Registers
entries.dateMeaning: First and last years in the digitized archival series
entries.summary: The surviving archive records ships and cargoes passing the Sound between the Baltic and North Sea.
entries.detail: The toll books make trade observable in a different way from imported objects. Surviving volumes vary by period, but entries can identify reported ports, cargo and duties.
entries.uncertainty: The years are archive coverage. Earlier toll collection is attested and the surviving series has gaps.

entries.title: Danish Reformation changes church government
entries.summary: The crown established a Lutheran settlement and reordered the church after civil conflict.
entries.detail: Church land, offices and religious education changed in ways that reached beyond the capital. The settlement created new settings for parish worship and administration.
entries.uncertainty: The year marks formal change. Religious practice and institutional reorganization followed different local timings.

entries.title: Renaissance building begins at Kronborg
entries.summary: Frederik II’s new construction at the narrow Sound began on an earlier castle site.
entries.detail: The position beside the shipping channel linked royal architecture, fortification and maritime revenue. The present ensemble also includes later rebuilding.
entries.uncertainty: The year dates the start of the Renaissance project. The earlier toll post and medieval castle have separate histories.

entries.title: A Danish trading station at Tranquebar
entries.dateMeaning: Years of the Danish station’s founding agreement and sale
entries.summary: A 1620 agreement with the ruler of Thanjavur enabled the Danish enterprise at Tharangambadi on India’s Coromandel Coast.
entries.detail: Known in Danish records as Tranquebar, the port involved Indian merchants, workers and institutions. Danish rule ended with a sale to the British in 1845.
entries.uncertainty: The straight map connection joins the documentary endpoints. The voyage itinerary and the extent of territorial authority changed over time.

entries.title: Copenhagen company establishes a base on St Thomas
entries.summary: The company based in Copenhagen established a colonial settlement in the Caribbean in 1672.
entries.detail: The wider Danish West Indies developed through plantation production, commerce and the forced labor of enslaved people. St Thomas also served as a trading and shipping center.
entries.uncertainty: The link gives company and island endpoints, with no claim that every voyage took the same route or that the treaty capacity matched control on the ground.

entries.title: A royal avenue links Copenhagen and Frederiksberg
entries.dateMeaning: Completion year reported in the city excavation history
entries.place: Vesterbrogade end of Frederiksberg Allé, with palace endpoint
entries.summary: The crown completed a private route between Copenhagen’s western approach and the new Frederiksberg Palace.
entries.detail: The avenue’s planned rows of trees and access rules made it a different kind of road from public paths. Archaeological investigation documents later roadside development.
entries.uncertainty: The endpoints are schematic. Completion in 1704 is separate from subsequent changes in access and building.

entries.title: Moravian community lays out Christiansfeld
entries.summary: A Moravian congregation established a planned settlement around a central square.
entries.detail: Buildings provided space for worship, shared housing and trades. The layout expressed a social organization that can be studied through the relationship between streets, working buildings and communal facilities.
entries.uncertainty: The year marks foundation while the conserved buildings were developed in stages.

entries.title: Copenhagen records 100,975 residents in the census
entries.summary: The 1 February count recorded 100,975 people in Copenhagen under the published historical city definition.
entries.detail: The city statistical yearbook separates Copenhagen from Frederiksberg and Gentofte. Counts from later metropolitan areas use larger and differing scopes.
entries.uncertainty: This is a historical enumeration for the Copenhagen column, which excludes separately listed neighbors.

population.note: Copenhagen column only, 1 February 1801 census, as reproduced in the City of Copenhagen statistical yearbook.

entries.title: Copenhagen–Roskilde railway opens
entries.summary: Passenger railway service opened between Copenhagen and Roskilde on Zealand.
entries.detail: The line made rail travel available from the capital and formed the beginning of a longer network. A railway had opened in 1844 in the then Danish monarchy’s Holstein territories.
entries.uncertainty: The connection joins the two opening places schematically. Later terminals and track rebuilding have distinct dates.

entries.title: The June Constitution is signed
entries.summary: The monarch signed a constitution that established a parliamentary framework and ended absolute monarchy.
entries.detail: The original document preserves the terms of the political change. Its rules left women and other groups outside the initial parliamentary electorate.
entries.uncertainty: The event dates signature. Constitutional coverage and later revisions require separate treatment.

entries.title: A death register documents Copenhagen’s cholera epidemic
entries.summary: A contemporary list recorded names, age, social position and dates of death for residents who died of cholera.
entries.detail: The register allows the epidemic to be studied through individuals and unequal living conditions, alongside aggregate deaths or later sanitary reforms.
entries.uncertainty: The citywide marker covers a documentary record. Household locations and completeness require reading its individual entries.

entries.title: Prussian forces capture the Dybbøl position
entries.summary: The fighting at Dybbøl was a decisive episode in the Second Schleswig War.
entries.detail: The protected landscape preserves evidence of different defensive works and phases. Treaties later changed sovereignty in Schleswig and Holstein.
entries.uncertainty: The point locates the battlefield area. The war’s settlements and changes of sovereignty have later dates.

entries.title: Workers and police confront each other at Fælleden
entries.summary: A labor gathering and police intervention became a formative episode for Denmark’s organized workers.
entries.detail: Meetings and printed agitation let workers coordinate beyond a single job site. The Workers Museum’s archives place the event in the wider development of associations.
entries.uncertainty: The point identifies the meeting district. Accounts reflect the standpoint of their participants and publishers.

entries.title: Workers open a Copenhagen assembly building
entries.summary: Worker organizations gained a building where they could hold meetings and social events.
entries.detail: The assembly rooms provided infrastructure for clubs, union activity and shared recreation. Later changes to the interior form distinct architectural phases.
entries.uncertainty: The year refers to the opening of the building. Individual organizations and uses each have their own history.

entries.title: Hjedding farmers establish a cooperative dairy
entries.summary: Farmers organized a shared processing enterprise for milk.
entries.detail: A cooperative could support common equipment and pooled production beyond the means of individual farms. The surviving dairy gives a local example of wider changes in rural labor and marketing.
entries.uncertainty: The map pin is a public locality anchor and the record dates the institution’s foundation.

entries.title: Copenhagen records 312,859 residents in the census
entries.summary: The 1 February census recorded 312,859 people in Copenhagen, using the city column of the published historical census series.
entries.detail: The same municipal series reports 100,975 for 1801. The two observations document urban growth over the nineteenth century and separately list Frederiksberg and other neighbors. Annexations around the turn of the twentieth century are accounted for separately in the yearbook.
entries.uncertainty: The comparison uses both published Copenhagen city observations. Historical municipal enumeration is not equivalent to a fixed modern metropolitan area.

population.note: Copenhagen column, 1 February 1890 enumeration, as reproduced in city yearbooks. Frederiksberg and other separately reported districts are excluded.

entries.title: Silver cauldron found while cutting peat
entries.dateMeaning: Year of documented recovery during peat cutting
entries.summary: Peat cutters uncovered pieces of a decorated silver vessel in the bog.
entries.detail: The recorded nineteenth-century find is a distinct event from the vessel’s Iron Age manufacture and deposition. Its workmanship and imagery raise questions about connections far beyond Denmark.
entries.uncertainty: The point is a find-area anchor and the dated event is recovery. The workshop and itinerary that brought the vessel to Denmark remain debated.

entries.title: An early camp at Saarenoja 2
entries.dateMeaning: Calibrated radiocarbon range of the burnt bone sample
entries.summary: A dated piece of burnt elk bone puts activity at this inland site early in the Mesolithic.
entries.detail: Stone tools and bone link early visitors to a landscape of recently deglaciated shorelines. Excavation produced an identifiable sample for radiocarbon dating.
entries.uncertainty: Approximate public district reference. The interval is the sample’s calibrated range, not the duration of the occupation.

entries.title: Blade-making at Sujala
entries.summary: Excavated blades and cores show early inland occupation in far northern Finland.
entries.detail: The tool technology invites comparison with assemblages to the east and with sites on the Norwegian coast. Ancient site distributions cross today’s frontiers.
entries.uncertainty: Broad public district point rather than detailed site location. The excavators offer a preferred date bracket from conflicting charcoal and bone evidence.

entries.title: Fishing villages along Kierikki’s changing shoreline
entries.summary: House depressions and artifacts record Neolithic settlements linked to fishing and exchange.
entries.detail: The river mouth and sea shore moved as the land rose. The people whose houses were found lived beside water at elevations that are inland today.
entries.uncertainty: The range describes several localities and episodes. Present-day distances to seawater are misleading guides to this period.

entries.title: Pictographs beside Lake Saimaa
entries.dateLabel: Middle to Late Neolithic, broadly fourth to third millennia BCE
entries.dateMeaning: Landscape and comparative dating of a group of pictographs
entries.summary: Repeated paintings on a rock face depict human and animal figures beside a lake route.
entries.detail: Researchers study the relation between the paintings, acoustics, shoreline access and the viewer’s approach from water or ice.
entries.uncertainty: The window is broad and based in part on lake-level histories. The meaning of any figure or practice remains interpretive.

entries.title: Stone cairns at Sammallahdenmäki
entries.summary: Large granite cairns were raised on a ridge near an earlier shoreline.
entries.detail: The cemetery includes many round cairns and structures with unusual outlines. Excavated examples differ in date and form.
entries.uncertainty: The window represents the coastal Bronze Age phase. Two excavated cairns are attributed to the Early Iron Age.

entries.title: Iron Age human remains at Levänluhta
entries.dateMeaning: Broad date of archaeological deposit and its studied people
entries.summary: Human remains and artifacts accumulated at a wet site in western Finland.
entries.detail: Bioarchaeology investigates the people whose remains survived, while local environmental changes help explain preservation. Different individuals show different histories.
entries.uncertainty: Approximate site district. The bracket describes the deposit and its dated remains. Ancient ancestry, language and modern Indigenous identity are separate questions.

entries.title: An eleventh-century burial at Luistari
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate burial date based on the archaeological assemblage
entries.summary: Grave 56 contains a furnished burial that researchers use to reconstruct aspects of Iron Age dress.
entries.detail: Surviving objects and traces of organic materials support interpretations of clothing and metal fittings. Modern reconstructions represent choices about fragmentary evidence.
entries.uncertainty: The dates concern the particular grave, not the whole cemetery. Reconstruction is distinct from the original finds.

entries.title: Turku Castle takes shape at the Aura mouth
entries.summary: The Swedish Crown began a fortified administrative site at the river mouth.
entries.detail: The river connected a developing town, coast and hinterland. The castle developed in stages as a royal and administrative complex.
entries.uncertainty: Points center on the castle, not its surrounding jurisdiction. Early construction and the first surviving documentary mention have distinct dates.

entries.title: The Great Coastal Road links Turku and Vyborg
entries.dateLabel: Likely from the 14th century, established in the late Middle Ages
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate medieval development and attestation of the route
entries.summary: A medieval overland road developed alongside the sea passage between Turku and Vyborg.
entries.detail: Heritage records trace sections through later villages and manors. Finnish and Russian placenames and state boundaries changed independently of the road’s early history.
entries.uncertainty: Start is an attribution in the heritage register. The link is a schematic endpoint pair, with later road changes and the shipping route distinct.

entries.title: Kastelholm Castle appears in surviving records
entries.dateMeaning: First documented mention of the castle
entries.summary: A surviving reference names the castle at Kastelholm during the Swedish realm’s medieval phase.
entries.detail: The island location made the castle part of interconnected waters and administrative networks. Parts of its structure were built or altered over several later phases.
entries.uncertainty: The first surviving reference is a documentary horizon. Construction and earlier local use have separate chronologies.

entries.title: A chartered town at Rauma
entries.summary: Rauma received town privileges in 1442.
entries.detail: The street network and trading role have medieval roots. Fires and later rebuilding explain why the visible wooden buildings mostly belong to later centuries.
entries.uncertainty: The year is the privileges date. It does not date the first local inhabitants or the surviving buildings.

entries.title: The Royal Academy opens at Turku
entries.summary: The Royal Academy of Turku was established during the Swedish period.
entries.detail: The institution trained clergy and officials. Study and publication connected Turku to other centres in the Baltic world.
entries.uncertainty: Location is a public city reference. The institution’s move to Helsinki in 1828 was a separate event.

entries.title: Building begins on the fortress islands
entries.summary: Sweden began the sea fortress on islands outside Helsinki.
entries.detail: Labor, materials, garrison households and naval facilities formed a substantial settlement alongside the defenses.
entries.uncertainty: The date is the beginning of construction. Individual forts, harbor works and later Russian alterations have separate dates.

entries.title: A wooden church for Petäjävesi
entries.summary: Local carpenters built a Lutheran church in the inland lake district.
entries.detail: The layout joined internationally circulating church forms with building traditions suited to logs. Travelers approached from land and lake.
entries.uncertainty: Construction dates follow the heritage description. A later bell tower is a separate building phase.

entries.title: Tar warehouses opened at Toppila
entries.summary: Tar for overseas shipment was stored in purpose-built warehouses.
entries.detail: The coast depended on household production and river transport from the forested hinterland. Port facilities concentrated the product for grading, loading and sale.
entries.uncertainty: The marker locates the port storage site. Individual inland supply routes and shipping voyages are outside this entry.

entries.title: The Diet of Porvoo convenes
entries.summary: Representatives of the estates and Alexander I met during the transfer from Swedish to Russian rule.
entries.detail: The grand duchy retained established laws and institutions in a changed relationship to imperial power. The Swedish-Russian peace settlement was separate from the meeting at Porvoo.
entries.uncertainty: This date and point refer to the Diet. They do not plot a frontier or identify the exact legal origin of every autonomous institution.

entries.title: A mill founded beside the Tammerkoski rapids
entries.summary: James Finlayson founded a factory in a town whose waterways supported industrial power.
entries.detail: The growing textile complex changed the pattern of work and housing. Later owners expanded machinery and employment far beyond the first shop.
entries.uncertainty: The date is the institutional founding, rather than a date for every textile activity or surviving building.

entries.title: The university transfers from Turku to Helsinki
entries.summary: The university moved to Helsinki in the year following the Great Fire of Turku.
entries.detail: Buildings in the new capital housed scholarly collections, teaching and administration. The fire and the relocation are separate moments.
entries.uncertainty: The marker indicates the university’s Helsinki locality, rather than the full area damaged by fire in Turku.

entries.title: A Finnish-language newspaper in Oulu
entries.summary: Evert Barck began publishing Oulun Wiikko-Sanomat in Finnish.
entries.detail: A local press expanded access to printed news in a city where Swedish remained important to many administrators and educated readers.
entries.uncertainty: The location refers to the city, not a known printing-room coordinate. It records a publication milestone, not a population-wide language shift.

entries.title: The first edition of the Kalevala
entries.place: Helsinki and the Finnish Literature Society
entries.summary: Elias Lönnrot arranged collected oral poetry into a literary edition issued in 1835.
entries.detail: Singers, collectors and publishers had different roles. The poems preserve material from several communities and recording journeys, including Karelia.
entries.uncertainty: Helsinki marks the publishing institution. Oral traditions come from a wider area and have earlier, independently dated histories.

entries.title: Passenger trains begin Helsinki–Hämeenlinna service
entries.summary: Scheduled passenger traffic began in March 1862 on Finland’s first railway.
entries.detail: The line carried travelers inland from the capital. The Railway Museum distinguishes the first route from the network’s later extensions.
entries.uncertainty: The endpoints represent a schematic rail link. The marker does not give the survey or later track geometry.

entries.title: Åström’s tannery opens at Myllytulli
entries.summary: The Åström brothers opened a tannery that later sold leather goods to the Russian market.
entries.detail: Production diversified from sole leather into footwear materials, machine belts and equipment. A factory changed the relation between craft work and wage employment.
entries.uncertainty: The location identifies the tannery district. Trade markets were geographically broad, so no single Russian endpoint is inferred.

entries.title: Harvest failure and famine mortality
entries.summary: Successive poor harvests contributed to high mortality across Finland.
entries.detail: Local evidence shows that the consequences differed by social conditions and access to resources. Hunger, disease and movement connected rural households and towns.
entries.uncertainty: Oulu is a regional comparison point. The cited study assesses mortality across local areas and the marker does not assign a local death total.

entries.title: Bridges link Oulujoki islands
entries.summary: Bridge works connected river islands at Oulu in 1869.
entries.detail: The crossings improved a local route over the river alongside the shipping and industrial economy.
entries.uncertainty: Marker and endpoint refer to the two named islands, not to measured bridge deck positions.

entries.title: A common school opens in Oulu
entries.summary: The city’s common school began with four teachers and 189 pupils in its first autumn.
entries.detail: A purpose-built school followed in 1876. The change left records of teaching and everyday life beyond the town’s port and trade histories.
entries.uncertainty: The numbers are first-term intake and staff, not a literacy rate or city population.

entries.title: Railway reaches Tampere from Hämeenlinna
entries.summary: An extension linked the first railway’s inland endpoint to industrial Tampere.
entries.detail: The railway connected new factories and households to a wider passenger and freight network.
entries.uncertainty: The endpoint connector is schematic and does not reproduce intermediate stations or surveyed geometry.

entries.title: Rebuilding a board mill at Verla
entries.summary: Operations resumed in 1882 after a fire destroyed the earlier mill.
entries.detail: The works processed wood near rapids and maintained a settlement around production. The buildings now visible belong to several rebuilding phases.
entries.uncertainty: The year identifies renewed operation, rather than the first paper-related production or construction of each building.

entries.title: People recorded in Tampere in 1900
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the published historical register total
entries.summary: The municipal statistical yearbook reports 43,832 people for Tampere in 1900.
entries.detail: The table sets Tampere beside surrounding municipalities and records people from church books and the civil register. Its figures are contemporary administrative categories.
entries.uncertainty: The count applies to the published Tampere category for that date and should not be compared to later expanded boundaries without adjustment.

population.note: Reported registered total, not a separate census event. The yearbook combines church books and the civil register, table 3.1B.

entries.title: Flintworking beside an early shoreline
entries.dateMeaning: Broad early coastal phase supported by archaeological and shoreline evidence
entries.summary: An early flint assemblage on present-day Rennesøy belongs to postglacial coastal settlement.
entries.detail: Comparative tool forms and reconstructed shorelines place the occupation in a wider pattern of coastal travel and repeated toolmaking.
entries.uncertainty: The broad rounded window provides early Holocene context. The dates and cultural assignment of the earliest Galta assemblages have been argued from several kinds of evidence.

entries.title: Early coastal camps at Pauler
entries.dateMeaning: Broad calibrated bracket for the pioneer period discussed with the Pauler sequence
entries.summary: Stone tools and dated occupation traces document early use of newly available coastal settings.
entries.detail: The dated phases belong to separate parts of a site complex and let investigators compare how activities on its changing shore were organized.
entries.uncertainty: Regional early Mesolithic bracket and approximate public locality. Individual camp visits are narrower and could be separated by long gaps.

entries.title: Human remains from Hummervikholmen
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded bracket for dated human remains
entries.summary: Human bones recovered from marine sediment preserve evidence of some of Norway’s early inhabitants.
entries.detail: Three individuals have been studied through archaeology and ancient DNA. The remains survived in an underwater setting and reveal aspects of life that stone tools alone cannot show.
entries.uncertainty: Approximate archipelago reference. The window rounds the dated finds and does not identify individual lifespans or a continuously occupied settlement.

entries.title: Alta Fjord rock art
entries.summary: Generation after generation carved and painted figures along the fjord’s changing shore.
entries.detail: People depicted boats, animals and scenes with human figures. Relative elevations and local shoreline history help distinguish different phases.
entries.uncertainty: The UNESCO range covers the complex as a whole. Individual images have separate readings and dates, and their makers’ identities are open questions.

entries.title: Boat carvings at Solbakk
entries.dateMeaning: Broad period attribution of the rock art
entries.summary: Carved boats dominate this shore-side rock-art site in Ryfylke.
entries.detail: The county’s account situates the imagery within Bronze Age southern Scandinavian rock art and local communities’ familiarity with the sea.
entries.uncertainty: The art indicates attention to boats. Dates come from the regional archaeological period and the lines do not identify a trading itinerary.

entries.title: Flagghaugen’s Roman Iron Age grave
entries.dateLabel: Later Roman Iron Age, about 200–400 CE
entries.dateMeaning: Archaeological period attribution of a specific grave
entries.summary: A wealthy grave at Avaldsnes contained gold and goods associated with contacts beyond the west Norwegian coast.
entries.detail: The grave stood beside a narrow navigation passage. Imported objects and local display signal connections and the resources commanded by one household.
entries.uncertainty: The burial has a period-level bracket. The find does not establish the territory of a specific ruler.

entries.title: A marketplace at Kaupang
entries.summary: Excavated plots and imported objects identify an early town and marketplace near Viksfjord.
entries.detail: Small finds capture household production and long-distance contacts that are less visible in spectacular burials. Foreign objects could pass through several hands before reaching Kaupang.
entries.uncertainty: Rounded trading phase. Excavated and inferred activity varied across individual plots.

entries.title: Fishing, farming and eider down at Vega
entries.dateMeaning: Broad historical tradition with an atlas display cutoff at 1900
entries.summary: Households combined fishing and modest farms with tending wild eiders for down.
entries.detail: People built and maintained small shelters for nesting birds. Women’s care and processing work was integral to an economy adapted to scattered, exposed islands.
entries.uncertainty: Ninth-century reporting concerns eider tending in Norway. The regional range represents a documented tradition, with different starting points on individual islands and continuation beyond 1900.

entries.title: Oseberg ship burial
entries.summary: Two women were buried with a ship, textiles, carved wood and other possessions.
entries.detail: The burial preserves the work of weaving and woodworking specialists as well as the elaborate display that accompanied the dead.
entries.uncertainty: The year is the burial date. Interpretations of individual identity and social role remain uncertain.

entries.title: Gokstad ship burial
entries.summary: A man was buried in a seagoing ship with equipment and animals.
entries.detail: The ship and burial have different histories. An elaborate grave can record choices about status and memory while putting a previously used vessel out of circulation.
entries.uncertainty: The window rounds the burial’s dating. The deceased’s personal identity is unconfirmed.

entries.title: Tune ship at Rolvsøy
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate date of the burial context
entries.summary: A clinker-built ship was laid in the large burial mound of Båthaugen.
entries.detail: Excavated in the nineteenth century, the vessel was heavily affected by early digging and conservation. Its surviving timbers still inform comparisons of construction.
entries.uncertainty: Public locality anchor near the findspot. The date concerns the burial context in the Viking Age, with an approximate early tenth-century assignment.

entries.title: Stone church begins at Nidaros
entries.summary: Olav Kyrre began a stone church at the place later occupied by Nidaros Cathedral.
entries.detail: The shrine of St Olav attracted pilgrims, artisans and governing institutions. Building and rebuilding continued for centuries.
entries.uncertainty: The date marks the stone church initiative as given by the cathedral. Many visible portions belong to later work.

entries.title: The stave church at Urnes
entries.dateLabel: First half of the 12th century CE
entries.summary: A wooden church on a fjord slope reused carving from an older building.
entries.detail: Carpenters expressed some of the proportions and forms of Romanesque stonebuilding in timber. The reused north portal records another phase of work.
entries.uncertainty: Rounded construction range of the standing medieval building. Some timbers and carvings have earlier histories.

entries.title: A royal stone church at Avaldsnes
entries.summary: Håkon Håkonsson’s period saw construction of a substantial stone church beside the Karmsund passage.
entries.detail: The project joined a royal residence landscape and a route used by vessels moving along the coast.
entries.uncertainty: Broad construction interval. The site anchor does not imply continuous control from the nearby Iron Age grave to the medieval church.

entries.title: Stockfish at Bergen’s Hanseatic wharf
entries.dateLabel: About the mid-14th to mid-16th century CE
entries.summary: Bergen’s wharf became a centre of Hanseatic trade and the export of dried fish.
entries.detail: Warehouses, merchant households and market rules connected the North Atlantic fish supply with continental merchants. The many later rebuilds show the durability of the plot pattern.
entries.uncertainty: Broad period of Hanseatic prominence. The location identifies the wharf and its local exchange, not the route of an individual cargo.

entries.title: Silver discovered near Kongsberg
entries.summary: The recorded 1623 silver find triggered the development of mining west of the later town.
entries.detail: The Crown developed a mining settlement, drawing technical knowledge and labor into the district.
entries.uncertainty: Point is at the mining district. Accounts of the original find are preserved partly as local tradition.

entries.title: Mining privileges around Røros
entries.summary: The Danish-Norwegian Crown issued privileges around the copper works.
entries.detail: Mines, smelters, farms, charcoal and transport formed one interdependent economy. Households in the outlying district participated through labor, fuel or hauling.
entries.uncertainty: The large historical privilege zone is described in the heritage source. The point marks the town and represents no boundary.

entries.title: Røros rebuilt after wartime destruction
entries.dateLabel: From the 1679 destruction into late-17th-century rebuilding
entries.dateMeaning: Documented destruction followed by an approximate reconstruction period
entries.summary: The town was rebuilt after Swedish troops destroyed it in 1679.
entries.detail: Laying out and rebuilding a remote mining town meant securing timber, supplies and labor while sustaining work at the mines.
entries.uncertainty: The end date rounds the first post-destruction reconstruction phase, not a building-by-building survey.

entries.title: Farmers organize around Kristian Lofthus
entries.summary: A movement associated with Kristian Lofthus petitioned about grievances in southern Norway.
entries.detail: Farmers raised issues connected with administration, trade and debt. The agitation linked multiple districts and became a confrontation with the authorities.
entries.uncertainty: The locality marks the leader’s district. It does not locate every petition signature or meeting.

entries.title: Kongevegen crosses Filefjell
entries.dateMeaning: Documented completion year of the earliest wheeled road over the pass
entries.summary: An engineered king’s road improved the overland passage between east and west Norway.
entries.detail: The surviving Filefjell sections show the amount of effort needed to make a wheeled road through a high mountain crossing.
entries.uncertainty: The map connects the pass with the west approach at Lærdal schematically. Historic roads and later alignments occupy different corridors.

entries.title: The constitution adopted at Eidsvoll
entries.summary: Representatives adopted the Norwegian Constitution in May 1814.
entries.detail: The constitution created a representative framework during upheaval at the end of the Napoleonic Wars. The subsequent union with Sweden required changes later that year.
entries.uncertainty: The point locates the assembly. It does not map the union or imply voting rights extended to the whole population.

entries.title: Emigrants depart Stavanger on Restauration
entries.summary: A small party left Stavanger for the United States aboard Restauration.
entries.detail: The crossing became a remembered starting point for organized nineteenth-century Norwegian emigration, although other Norwegian emigrants preceded it.
entries.uncertainty: The marker is the documented departure. A symbolic landing or reconstructed track has not been added.

entries.title: Workers’ associations grow from Drammen
entries.summary: Marcus Thrane helped organize the first workers’ association in a wider network of clubs.
entries.detail: Members and organizers petitioned over political participation and social conditions. The associations spread under a franchise that excluded many members.
entries.uncertainty: The point marks the founding city, not the full reach of the associations.

entries.title: Women in Akerselva textile work
entries.dateLabel: Second half of the 19th century CE
entries.summary: River-side textile factories employed women alongside men and children in a growing industrial district.
entries.detail: Water power, buildings, housing and shifts bound factory labor to the river. Museum collections preserve evidence of different positions within the workforce.
entries.uncertainty: The range describes the industrial transformation treated by the museum. It is not an employment series or a date for every mill.

entries.title: Railway opens from Christiania to Eidsvoll
entries.summary: The Hovedbanen opened from Christiania to Eidsvoll in 1854.
entries.detail: Rail traffic linked the capital to a northern interchange and altered the movement of passengers and goods.
entries.uncertainty: Endpoints are schematic and do not reproduce the historical alignment. The opening date does not date later extensions.

entries.title: Parliamentary government takes hold
entries.summary: A political crisis in 1884 marked the breakthrough of parliamentary government.
entries.detail: The relationship between ministry and Storting changed as the executive increasingly depended on a parliamentary majority.
entries.uncertainty: The location is the parliamentary seat. This constitutional convention developed through practice after 1884.

entries.title: Norway extends the vote to men regardless of property
entries.summary: Parliament adopted general male suffrage in 1898.
entries.detail: The measure followed successive changes in eligibility. Women’s national suffrage came later, and other administrative conditions continued to matter.
entries.uncertainty: The location is the legislative seat, not a constituency-level map of participation.

entries.title: Postglacial coastal use in Varanger
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded earliest archaeological horizon in the Varanger landscape
entries.summary: Ancient shore levels in the Varanger landscape retain traces of early settlement and resource use.
entries.detail: The Varanger Sámi Museum explains how land uplift redistributed beaches, settlement places and access to coastal resources. The site preserves later Sámi cultural remains as well as much earlier activity.
entries.uncertainty: The broad timeframe summarizes earliest phases in the heritage landscape. It does not assign modern identities or a language to the oldest deposits.

entries.title: Alpine dwelling foundations in Devddesvuopmi
entries.summary: Low circular dwelling foundations survive in a wider mountain landscape used by Sámi communities.
entries.detail: Comparative archaeology distinguishes one concentrated period of stállo-style dwellings from later turf-house floors. Dwelling sites, paths and hunting evidence can be read together across present-day national borders.
entries.uncertainty: The dates describe the comparative construction cluster. The placement is a broad upland anchor and the precise economic role of these dwellings remains debated.

entries.title: Skolt Sámi community preserves written resource rights
entries.dateMeaning: First and last surviving documents in the archive
entries.summary: Surviving imperial edicts confirm a Skolt Sámi community’s rights to fishing and herding territories.
entries.detail: The community safeguarded a portable archive and maintained knowledge of where it was kept. The surviving materials have since traveled through different national archives and were returned to Sámi archival care.
entries.uncertainty: These are the dates of the surviving records. The location is a district anchor and the community’s earlier use extends beyond the archive.

entries.title: Winter market at Jåhkåmåhkke / Jokkmokk
entries.summary: A state-organized winter market became a place for Sámi trade, gatherings and official encounters.
entries.detail: The market brought together exchange, taxation and administration. Its continuing history also reflects the ways Sámi visitors have made and remade it as a gathering place.
entries.uncertainty: The year refers to the institution’s first recorded market, while trade and gatherings existed earlier.

entries.title: Skyttean school operates in Lycksele
entries.summary: The Skyttean school educated Sámi boys in a mission and church setting.
entries.detail: Its history sits alongside early printed Sámi-language materials and the development of written forms. A school’s language practices are one way to examine how ecclesiastical policies reached households.
entries.uncertainty: The dates mark the school’s operation. It served a selected group of children and does not represent all Sámi education.

entries.title: Nasafjäll silver mining and compelled transport
entries.dateMeaning: Start and end years of the initial mine operation
entries.place: Nasafjäll / Násávárre mining district, approximate anchor
entries.summary: The Swedish crown opened a mountain silver mine and drew on Sámi people and reindeer for transport.
entries.detail: Mining required extracting and moving ore through a highland landscape. Although state arrangements included compensation, the assigned transport burdens were coercive and disrupted other livelihoods.
entries.uncertainty: The interval concerns the initial operation, distinct from later attempts to reopen the mine. The mark locates the district broadly.

entries.title: A survey records Sámi tax lands in Västerbotten
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the historical land survey
entries.summary: A survey inventoried tax lands associated with Sámi households and communities.
entries.detail: Fiscal records can preserve evidence of recognized uses, named places and resource access. They reflect Crown administrative goals and have to be read alongside local sources.
entries.uncertainty: The survey was regional. This point identifies a reference district and no surveyed land boundaries are inferred.

entries.title: A trading post opens at Mortensnes
entries.summary: A documented Norwegian trading post became one more layer in a long-used Sámi coastal landscape.
entries.detail: Its establishment gave exchange an institutional foothold alongside existing fishing, herding and household use. The heritage dossier compares it with other trading and settlement sites around Varanger.
entries.uncertainty: The date concerns the post. Earlier exchange and the territorial consequences are separate historical questions.

entries.title: Border treaty recognizes customary Sámi crossings
entries.place: Deatnu / Tana boundary region, illustrative locality
entries.summary: The Norway–Sweden border treaty included a codicil addressing longstanding Sámi access across the new frontier.
entries.detail: In a landscape already used seasonally, the Lapp Codicil addressed crossings and use of established pastures under an interstate treaty. The archival record gives a dated legal change.
entries.uncertainty: The point locates a northern section of the affected boundary region. It is neither the signing location nor a surveyed boundary line.

entries.title: Vardø trades with Russian White Sea ports
entries.dateMeaning: Century of peak activity described by the museum
entries.summary: Pomor crews supplied northern Norway and exchanged goods with coastal traders and fishers.
entries.detail: The Varanger Museum describes Arkhangelsk as a center of the White Sea trading area and the nineteenth century as a peak phase in Vardø. Preserved wharf buildings give material evidence for what was stored and handled at port.
entries.uncertainty: The endpoints identify documented network hubs. Pomor traders used multiple ports, and no precise sailing line or continuous trade volume is implied.

entries.title: Norway and Russia delimit their eastern frontier
entries.summary: A boundary agreement and demarcation changed the status of a district with overlapping jurisdiction and resource uses.
entries.detail: Before the settlement, access to fishing and taxable resources produced overlapping claims and disputes. The border is one of several different phases that changed mobility across eastern Sápmi.
entries.uncertainty: The anchor is within the border district. The agreement is separate from local land use and later changes to adjacent frontiers.

entries.title: Laestadian revival takes hold around Karesuando
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate growth of the first revival activity
entries.summary: Preaching associated with Lars Levi Læstadius gained a following in a multilingual Sámi and Finnish-speaking region.
entries.detail: The revival grew through local congregations and lay networks across what are now Sweden, Finland and Norway. Followers adapted and disseminated it through their own languages and social relationships.
entries.uncertainty: The year is a rounded starting horizon and religious affiliation varied across communities.

entries.title: Timbers date a coastal Sámi boathouse in Høybukt
entries.dateLabel: Second half of the nineteenth century CE
entries.dateMeaning: Construction period inferred from tree-ring analysis
entries.summary: Tree-ring work dates the construction of a surviving Sámi boathouse to the later nineteenth century.
entries.detail: The building is a material record of coastal work, maintenance and reused structures. Varanger Museum and the Sámi Parliament collaborated in dating the timber.
entries.uncertainty: The range follows the museum’s construction summary. The pin shows the bay district, not precise private or sensitive building coordinates.

entries.title: State funding promotes Norwegian in Sámi and Kven schools
entries.dateMeaning: Year the national education funding line was established
entries.place: Hammerfest school district, documented local context
entries.summary: Norway established the budget line commonly called Finnefondet to promote education in Norwegian.
entries.detail: The resulting programs affected Sámi and Kven children. The Hammerfest school history gives examples of how rural school districts sought funding as instruction policies changed.
entries.uncertainty: The decision was national. The place identifies a documented later context for local use of the fund.

entries.title: Finland–Norway frontier closes to reindeer movements
entries.place: Utsjoki / Ohcejohka and Deatnu area, affected district anchor
entries.summary: The border closure disrupted customary seasonal movements and constrained access to pasture across the frontier.
entries.detail: Herders needed to reorganize access to grazing, negotiate with authorities or change routes. The implications differed by location and among households.
entries.uncertainty: The point marks a relevant border district. The closure had varied consequences and travel conditions changed further in later decades.

entries.title: Uprising in Guovdageaidnu / Kautokeino
entries.summary: An uprising led by a group of Sámi people killed a merchant and a local official and was followed by severe state reprisals.
entries.detail: The sources place the event amid trading relationships, religious revival, previous prosecutions and changes affecting herders. Sámi Archives provides context and original records, including the priest’s report.
entries.uncertainty: Official reports and testimony represent different perspectives. A single cause cannot account for the event.

entries.title: Swedish reindeer grazing law reshapes rights
entries.place: Jokkmokk, illustrative locality in the affected region
entries.summary: A Swedish law reorganized reindeer grazing rights around collective administrative units.
entries.detail: It formally shifted the relationship between individual or household use and collective rights. Sámi people with other livelihoods experienced different effects from families registered for herding.
entries.uncertainty: The law applied across several districts and this map point only locates one affected Sámi center.

entries.title: A Sámi Orthodox chapel in the Lovozero tundra is rebuilt
entries.place: Lovozero district, Kola Peninsula, regional anchor
entries.summary: Archival research identifies enlargement and renovation of a chapel associated with a Sámi churchyard on the Kola Peninsula.
entries.detail: The surviving structure and related records link Russian Orthodox history to the local choices of a Sámi community. They show activity on the eastern side of Sápmi alongside other religious histories farther west.
entries.uncertainty: The date concerns renovation and the original construction is less certain. The map shows the administrative district and omits the exact site.

entries.title: A Norwegian school instruction restricts Sámi and Kven use
entries.place: Northern school districts, Hammerfest reference point
entries.summary: The instruction associated with Vilhelm Andreas Wexelsen tightened limits on the use of Sámi and Kven at school.
entries.detail: Norwegianization developed through funding, curricula and individual schools’ enforcement. Children and teachers experienced the changes differently, and languages continued to be spoken in families and communities.
entries.uncertainty: The date is the formal instruction. The marker gives a local school context and does not imply uniform enforcement.

entries.title: Barentsz’s expedition documents Bjørnøya
entries.summary: The surviving voyage account places the Dutch expedition at Bjørnøya on 10 June 1596.
entries.detail: The crew was searching for a navigable maritime connection toward Asian markets. Their descriptions and maps later circulated more widely than the voyage itself.
entries.uncertainty: The record is an early documented encounter. The pin locates the island, with the exact ship position and any prior sightings unspecified.

entries.title: The Dutch expedition records mountainous land near 80° north
entries.summary: On 17 June the Dutch party sighted and subsequently described the land they called Spitsbergen.
entries.detail: Its reported latitude, profile of pointed mountains and subsequent movement along the west coast became part of early European geographic knowledge about the archipelago.
entries.uncertainty: The regional pin is not a reconstructed sighting position. The evidence supports a documented encounter rather than an exhaustive account of earlier visits.

entries.title: Systematic bowhead whaling begins
entries.dateMeaning: Conventional start of systematic whale hunting in the museum account
entries.summary: Organized voyages took whales and processed blubber to supply European oil markets.
entries.detail: Early hunting took place from vessels with land-based processing in suitable coastal locations. Svalbard Museum cites captain Thomas Edge and other early voyage records to situate the industry.
entries.uncertainty: The museum uses 1612 for the start of systematic whaling, in contrast with earlier visits and takes. The marker is an illustrative coastal point.

entries.title: Smeerenburg workers render whale oil on Amsterdamøya
entries.summary: Shore crews used ovens and other installations to process whale blubber during seasonal occupations.
entries.detail: Archaeological remains preserve evidence of coordinated work, equipment and provisions under difficult coastal conditions. The site belonged to a broader set of processing stations.
entries.uncertainty: This is a rounded primary phase for the shore station. Use started before the early bound and archaeological remains represent different moments.

entries.title: Volunteers winter at the whaling station
entries.dateMeaning: Beginning year of the documented winter stay
entries.summary: Seven volunteers were left at Smeerenburg to winter in 1634, an unusually detailed example of early seasonal work becoming a full winter stay.
entries.detail: The comparison of Atlantic Arctic winterings uses contemporary records to examine supply and shelter. Difficulties faced by stay-behind groups differed from those of summer crews.
entries.uncertainty: The year is when the documented wintering began. Seasonal work at the station dates more broadly.

entries.title: Pomor crews occupy winter trapping stations
entries.dateMeaning: Museum’s regional range for Russian winter trapping
entries.place: Russekeila, Isfjorden coast, example of a wider network
entries.summary: Russian Arctic hunters used shore stations and winter structures alongside summer resource gathering.
entries.detail: The Svalbard Museum’s regional chronology can be read with the Governor’s site catalogue. Russekeila contains building foundations and other remains of Russian activity, within a larger archipelago-wide system.
entries.uncertainty: The dates are regional, not assigned to every occupation layer at Russekeila. The station pin represents a wider network of distinct sites.

entries.title: A Hammerfest firm sponsors an early Norwegian wintering
entries.dateMeaning: Years of the documented Norwegian wintering season
entries.summary: The Buch company equipped fifteen men for what the Svalbard Museum identifies as the first Norwegian overwintering expedition.
entries.detail: Information from Pomor hunters influenced Norwegian trapping activity. Later winter camps combined resource extraction with day-to-day work to keep people warm, fed and connected to supplies.
entries.uncertainty: The museum establishes the season and sponsor. The point is regional context, rather than an identification of a camp or route.

entries.title: Nineteenth-century wintering evidence at Skolteneset
entries.dateMeaning: Year associated with the severe winter at the station
entries.summary: Archaeological finds, including a wooden comb, illuminate material life at a Pomor trapping station.
entries.detail: The museum connects the station with a severe winter in which a crew died. Personal equipment highlights the lived experience of people often visible in records chiefly through hunting totals and vessel accounts.
entries.uncertainty: The year dates the museum’s documented winter episode, while the archaeological object has its own context.

entries.title: Fram emerges from the drifting ice near Danskøya
entries.summary: Otto Sverdrup and the crew freed Fram from the ice near Danskøya on 13 August 1896.
entries.detail: The ship’s return followed an extended drift intended to test ocean and ice movement. Nansen and Johansen had left it earlier and reached the mainland by a separate route.
entries.uncertainty: The point marks the reported island vicinity and does not reconstruct the moving ice or ship’s complete track.

entries.title: A steamship company builds a hotel at Hotellneset
entries.summary: Vesteraalens Dampskipsselskap built a hotel at the point now called Hotellneset.
entries.detail: The venture joined steamship access to accommodation and reflects a nineteenth-century tourism history alongside resource extraction and polar expeditions. A small site could have very different meanings to visitors and workers.
entries.uncertainty: The construction year dates the hotel, not the earliest visit by a traveler or ship.

entries.title: Andrée’s party reaches Kvitøya
entries.summary: After their balloon came down and they continued on the ice, the expedition members reached Kvitøya in early October.
entries.detail: Records recovered much later supplied evidence for their final camp and the end of the expedition. Weather, pack ice and the distance from regular shipping shaped their prospects.
entries.uncertainty: The late season and locality are documented. The exact causes and sequence of the deaths remain uncertain.

entries.title: Andrée’s balloon departs from Virgohamna
entries.summary: The hydrogen balloon Örnen left Virgohamna on 11 July with Salomon August Andrée, Nils Strindberg and Knut Frænkel.
entries.detail: The Governor’s catalogue preserves evidence of the expedition’s infrastructure, and the museum presents the diary-based account. Wind conditions had prevented an attempt the previous season.
entries.uncertainty: The site marks the launch location. The crew lost steering equipment and its subsequent movements need separate source-based positions.

entries.title: Trondheim entrepreneurs occupy the coalfields at Adventfjorden
entries.place: Adventfjorden coalfield, present Longyearbyen mining area
entries.summary: A group from Trondheim occupied coalfields in the valley south of Adventfjorden and formed a company.
entries.detail: The 1900 claim marks one stage before major industrial settlement. Operations, buildings and population changed substantially over the following decades.
entries.uncertainty: The point identifies the coalfield vicinity rather than an exact legal polygon. Longyear City and current Norwegian sovereignty belong to later phases.

entries.title: Late Ice Age flint point from Bohuslän
entries.summary: A tanged flint point from Torskär represents Late Palaeolithic activity on the west coast.
entries.detail: The Swedish History Museum identifies the object’s material as flint and gives its find locality as Torskär, Bohuslän. The shaft displayed with it is a reconstruction.
entries.uncertainty: The point has a broad typological date. The map pin locates coastal Bohuslän, not the individual findspot or an excavated settlement.

entries.title: Early lakeshore activity at Motala
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate age of surviving activity evidence
entries.summary: Traces near Motala attest early Holocene activity beside a changing lake and river system.
entries.detail: The Swedish History Museum dates early evidence here to about 9000 BCE. The location is an anchor for activity across the waterway landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The rounded age dates surviving traces, and people may have been there earlier.

entries.title: Early postglacial activity at Aareavaara
entries.summary: Early evidence from far northern Sweden shows occupation soon after ice retreat.
entries.detail: Aareavaara complements the southern record at Motala. The museum uses it to explain how people entered recently deglaciated landscapes from more than one direction.
entries.uncertainty: The village-area pin and rounded date summarize a site complex. The evidence gives no language or national affiliation.

entries.title: Living and burying beside the Skateholm lagoon
entries.summary: Hearths, food waste, structures and several cemeteries survive beside a former lagoon.
entries.detail: An elderly man and a child were laid facing each other in one of the graves. Amber and perforated bear teeth accompanied the child. The surrounding finds allow comparison of funerary activity and everyday use.
entries.uncertainty: The span covers use of several lagoon sites. Individual burials have their own dates and relationships among people in the graves are uncertain.

entries.title: A wooden platform in the Alvastra mire
entries.summary: People laid down timber and drove piles into a wetland beside a spring.
entries.detail: The preserved platform connected by a causeway affords unusual insight into working wood, building and the selective placement of objects in the Neolithic. The museum research archive publishes excavation records.
entries.uncertainty: The construction date is rounded and why people gathered there remains debated.

entries.title: Bronze Age rock carvings at Tanum
entries.summary: Rock panels depict boats, figures and other motifs in a landscape whose shoreline has changed.
entries.detail: The carving clusters preserve repeated encounters with particular outcrops. The boats give evidence of the importance of waterborne life while the panels themselves were made by multiple communities and generations.
entries.uncertainty: Dates describe a broad archaeological period. Individual images may be much harder to date or interpret.

entries.title: A long-lived central place at Uppåkra
entries.summary: Repeated rebuilding, craft remains and imported objects mark a large Iron Age central place near modern Lund.
entries.detail: The excavations provide evidence of connections across Europe, local metalwork and buildings used over successive phases. Parts of the settlement remain below farmland.
entries.uncertainty: Both ends are rounded. The political status and occupied extent changed over the centuries.

entries.title: Monumental mounds at Gamla Uppsala
entries.summary: Large burial mounds commemorate people associated with a regional center.
entries.detail: Excavation finds place important mound activity in the sixth century. Nearby buildings, smaller graves and later churches give this place a history much longer than the construction of the largest monuments.
entries.uncertainty: Traditional attributions to named kings have uncertain historical support.

entries.title: Birka marketplace on Björkö
entries.dateLabel: Mid-eighth to late tenth century CE
entries.summary: A waterfront settlement linked craft producers and merchants to Baltic and more distant networks.
entries.detail: Birka and the estate at Hovgården on Adelsö preserve complementary evidence for exchange, settlement and power. Imported objects establish connectivity at different scales.
entries.uncertainty: The map shows Birka on Björkö. The dating is an editorial approximation of the archaeological urban phase.

entries.title: Hanseatic trade at Visby
entries.summary: Merchant houses and warehouses reflect Visby’s role in Baltic trade.
entries.detail: The walled town’s surviving buildings attest commercial wealth, while its position on Gotland made it a meeting point for merchants from multiple shores.
entries.uncertainty: The span reflects the trading phase discussed by UNESCO. It gives no year-by-year limit of the town’s reach.

entries.title: Mining at the Great Copper Mountain
entries.dateLabel: Copper mining attested by the thirteenth century
entries.summary: Copper production involved mines, smelters and a changing landscape of farms and workers’ housing.
entries.detail: The documentary and archaeological sources together place early production before the later international peak. The mine, nearby settlements and industrial remains form a larger working landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The early interval is a documented horizon. It cannot identify a year when extraction began.

entries.title: Stockholm named in surviving letters
entries.summary: Letters provide the earliest preserved mentions of Stockholm.
entries.detail: The location links Lake Mälaren and the Baltic. The archival record gives a secure year for the use of the name, amid a longer process of settlement and urban development.
entries.uncertainty: The documentary mention is a terminus for the name. Establishing when the settlement began requires archaeology and other evidence.

entries.title: Nordic union ceremony at Kalmar
entries.summary: Erik of Pomerania was crowned over Denmark, Norway and Sweden in a joint ceremony.
entries.detail: The union under one ruler coexisted with separate institutions, regional rivalries and intermittent political control. Kalmar is the place of the ceremony and union documents.
entries.uncertainty: Authority changed over time and across territories. The point does not imply a single uniform state footprint.

entries.title: Church-going and lodging at Gammelstad
entries.dateMeaning: Century of the medieval parish church
entries.summary: A parish church drew people from scattered farms into a shared seasonal meeting place.
entries.detail: The medieval church predates many of the preserved timber cottages. The clustered lodgings housed people temporarily for church observances and other occasions when long distances made same-day travel difficult.
entries.uncertainty: The mapped window dates the church phase and the surviving cottages span later centuries.

entries.title: Uppsala University founded
entries.summary: A church-linked university began teaching in Uppsala.
entries.detail: Written privileges and a founding ceremony mark an institutional opening, creating a northern place for advanced study. Early university activity had interruptions, particularly through political and ecclesiastical change.
entries.uncertainty: The pin marks medieval Uppsala broadly. The modern university buildings belong to later phases.

entries.title: Vasa sinks on its first voyage
entries.summary: The new warship sank within the harbor on its departure.
entries.detail: Finds from the preserved vessel illuminate shipbuilding and everyday objects used around the crew. The sinking itself is documented independently of the twentieth-century recovery.
entries.uncertainty: The pin is an approximate harbor location for the sinking. The ship now stands at a museum elsewhere in Stockholm.

entries.title: Ironworking at Engelsberg
entries.summary: Furnaces, workshops and houses survive from a water-powered ironworks.
entries.detail: The industrial landscape tied charcoal supply, ore and labor to streams and transport. Engelsberg preserves a coordinated set of production buildings from the period when Swedish iron was widely exported.
entries.uncertainty: The map interval identifies an important early phase, not the full duration of ironworking in the area.

entries.title: A new naval port at Karlskrona
entries.summary: The Swedish crown founded a new naval base and town in its southern archipelago.
entries.detail: The dockyard and planned streets connected state demand to construction, maintenance and the work of a permanent naval town. Building continued well beyond the founding year.
entries.uncertainty: The initial date marks the town’s foundation. The port was assembled in stages.

entries.title: Göteborg merchants trade at Canton
entries.dateMeaning: Years of the documented first Swedish East India Company voyage
entries.summary: The first Swedish East India Company voyage carried a commercial delegation to Guangzhou, known in European records as Canton.
entries.detail: Colin Campbell’s diary documents the outward venture and the company’s early operations. Guangzhou was home to merchants, brokers and port workers who made the exchange possible.
entries.uncertainty: The endpoints connect documented markets. They leave the sailing itinerary, intermediate stops and historical waterfront locations unspecified.

entries.title: Göta Canal opens
entries.summary: The completed canal made a new inland water connection across southern Sweden.
entries.detail: The system linked artificial cuts and locks to lakes, connecting inland towns more closely to Baltic and western navigation. Motala was a construction and industrial center on the canal.
entries.uncertainty: The marker stands for an infrastructure system, and the year dates completion. Work began earlier.

entries.title: A Katarina infant school admissions ledger
entries.dateMeaning: Year represented in the archival record
entries.summary: A ledger preserves evidence of children entering organized care.
entries.detail: The 1843 entries record names, birth dates, residences and parents’ occupations for young children enrolled in a school that provided care while their parents worked.
entries.uncertainty: The surviving ledger records selected children. It gives neither citywide coverage nor each child’s later life.

entries.title: Rail passenger service between Malmö and Lund
entries.summary: A state main-line section opened between Malmö and Lund.
entries.detail: The opening formed part of Sweden’s first generation of public railways. The neighboring towns could now be linked by a timetable rather than only by existing roads and coastal traffic.
entries.uncertainty: The line connects the two documented towns schematically. The period alignment and station sites require a historical map.

entries.title: Western Main Line joins Göteborg and Stockholm
entries.summary: The completed Western Main Line linked Sweden’s two largest ports and cities across the interior.
entries.detail: Several segments opened earlier, and the final connection changed the regional options for inland goods and passenger journeys.
entries.uncertainty: The endpoint line is schematic. Opening events on predecessor sections are separate dates.

entries.title: Brännkyrka parish school rules take effect
entries.dateMeaning: Year the city archive identifies for the established regulations
entries.summary: A set of school rules establishes how authorities expected children to behave and attend.
entries.detail: The governing body adopted the school plan in late 1865. The city archive labels the rules as established in 1866. They cover instruction, discipline, holidays and teachers’ obligations in a district that was then rural.
entries.uncertainty: The city pin locates the document’s administrative setting. A written rule provides incomplete evidence of enforcement.

entries.title: Railways switch to Swedish standard time
entries.summary: A common Swedish time replaced the railway’s separate time convention.
entries.detail: Rail coordination exposed the difference between local solar times and a single timetable across long distances. Standard time affected both trains and the people who planned around them.
entries.uncertainty: The marker shows a national network hub, while the change applied across the system.

entries.title: Sawmill workers strike around Sundsvall
entries.summary: Workers from multiple mills stopped work in a dispute over wages and conditions.
entries.detail: The coast’s timber industry employed workers across dispersed mill villages. Their coordinated action and the authorities’ response left documentary evidence of the growing industrial labor force.
entries.uncertainty: The strike had multiple locations. Sundsvall is a district anchor rather than a single rendezvous.

entries.title: Stockholm reaches about 300,000 inhabitants
entries.dateMeaning: Year of the published city population comparison
entries.summary: The city archive reports about 300,000 inhabitants in 1900, up from about 90,000 in 1850.
entries.detail: Industry and housing grew alongside arrivals from the countryside and other towns. The two rounded numbers illustrate the scale of nineteenth-century urbanization.
entries.uncertainty: The published comparison uses rounded city populations. Its figures do not describe the metropolitan area.

population.note: The city archive gives a rounded figure of 300,000; the repeated value preserves its reporting precision and does not assert an exact count.
